facts.fact_text: The applicant party, the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP), is a parliamentary political party in the Republic of Moldova.

On 26 December 2001, the parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) informed Chișinău Municipal Council of its intention to hold a meeting with its supporters on 9 January 2002.
The meeting planned by the CDPP parliamentary group for 9 January 2002 was to be held in Great National Assembly Square, in front of the government buildings.
The CDPP parliamentary group stated that the meeting planned for 9 January 2002 would relate to the introduction of the compulsory study of Russian in schools.
On 9 January 2002, the parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) held a gathering in Great National Assembly Square, in front of government headquarters.
The parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) also held gatherings on 11, 13, 15, 16 and 17 January 2002.
No signs of violence can be seen in the video submitted by the Government of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.

On 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued an official warning to the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) in accordance with section 27 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice warned the CDPP that if it failed to comply with the warning, the Ministry would impose a temporary ban (suspendarea activităţii) on the party's activities in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act.

On 18 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued a decision imposing a one-month ban on the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP)'s activities, in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.

On 23 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council addressed a letter to the Ministry of Justice informing it that there was a discrepancy between the provisions of the Status of Members of Parliament Act and those of the Assemblies Act.

In its letter of 23 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council informed the Ministry of Justice that it did not know which of the two Acts — the Status of Members of Parliament Act or the Assemblies Act — to apply.

On 26 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council issued a decision noting that the provisions of domestic legislation were contradictory in respect of the demonstrations organised by the CDPP and that the opinions of legal experts were contradictory.

In its decision of 26 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council stated that it had formally requested the Ministry of Justice to ask Parliament for an official and urgent interpretation of the relevant legislation.
In its decision of 26 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council suspended its decision of 3 January 2002 until Parliament had given its official interpretation of the relevant legislation.

On 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued an official warning to the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) in accordance with section 27 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.

On 18 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued a decision imposing a one-month ban on the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP)'s activities, in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP's actions disclosed a violation of sections 27 and 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.
Section 5 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted only after the organisers have notified the local council.

Section 27 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 provides that in the event that breaches of the statute or of the law are discovered in the activities of a party or a socio-political organisation, the Ministry of Justice shall warn its leaders in writing, requesting that the breaches be remedied within a fixed time-limit.

Section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 (as originally enacted) provides that the Ministry of Justice shall impose a temporary ban on the activities of a party or socio-political organisation which breaches the provisions of the Constitution or those of the Act, or does not comply with a warning.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP had breached the provisions of sections 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11 of the Assemblies Act by not obtaining prior authorisation from Chișinău Municipal Council to stage demonstrations.
According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP had breached the provisions of sections 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11 of the Assemblies Act by blocking the public highway.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of Article 15 of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of section 13(3) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994.
According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of section 56(g) of the Education Act of 21 July 1995.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the use of the slogan 'I'd rather be dead than a communist' (Mai bine mort decât comunist) could be interpreted as a call to public violence and an act undermining the legal and constitutional order.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal stated that as a result of the CDPP demonstrations, the public transport company had suffered losses of 12,133 Moldovan lei (MDL), equivalent to approximately 1,050 euros (EUR) at the time.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal found that the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989, the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 and the Education Act of 21 July 1995.

On 18 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued a decision imposing a one-month ban on the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP)'s activities, in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.
On 8 February 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued a decision lifting the temporary ban imposed on the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP)'s activities.
The Ministry of Justice lifted the temporary ban on the CDPP's activities following an inquiry by the Secretary General of the Council of Europe under Article 52 of the Convention.
The Ministry of Justice lifted the temporary ban on the CDPP's activities having regard to the forthcoming local elections.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal of the Republic of Moldova found in favour of the Ministry of Justice and ruled that the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002 imposing a one-month ban on the CDPP's activities had been lawful.

On 17 May 2002, a panel of the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Moldova delivered its judgment dismissing the appeal lodged by the CDPP against the Court of Appeal's decision of 7 March 2002.
In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice found that since the demonstrations organised by the CDPP had been illegal, the sanction imposed on it had not been disproportionate.

In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice stated that in any event the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002 had not had any negative effects on the CDPP since it had not been enforced, the CDPP's accounts had not been frozen and the party could continue its activities unhindered.
The gatherings shown in the video submitted by the Government were held in Great National Assembly Square, in a pedestrian area, in front of the government buildings.
It appears from the video submitted by the Government that traffic was not disrupted as a result of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
No signs of violence can be seen in the video submitted by the Government of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
